stemBlocks.value: The diagram shows kite ABCD, where AB = AD, CB = CD, and the diagonal AC is drawn. a) Prove that triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ADC, stating the congruence case used. b) Hence show that AC bisects ∠BAD. c) If ∠ABC = 68°, determine ∠ADC.
Think first: The diagonal AC belongs to both triangles, so it supplies the third pair of equal sides for free.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p165-q03 from workbook page 165.

solutionSteps.instruction: List the equal sides in triangles ABC and ADC.

contentBlocks.value: AB = AD (given); CB = CD (given); AC = AC (common side)
Result: three pairs of equal sides
All three sides of one triangle equal all three sides of the other
∠BAC and ∠DAC are corresponding angles of the congruent triangles, so they are equal
AC splits ∠BAD into two equal parts

solutionSteps.instruction: Match the angles at B and D.

contentBlocks.value: ∠ABC and ∠ADC are corresponding angles of the congruent triangles

strategyBlocks.value: List the three pairs of equal sides to establish SSS congruence, then read off the equal corresponding angles for parts b and c.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) Triangle ABC ≅ triangle ADC by SSS (AB = AD, CB = CD, AC common)  (b) ∠BAC = ∠DAC as corresponding angles of congruent triangles, so AC bisects ∠BAD  (c) ∠ADC = 68°

whyThisWorks.value: Congruence means the two triangles are identical copies, so every matched part — side, angle, area — is equal. Once SSS is established, no further calculation is needed for parts b and c: the equal angles are simply corresponding parts being read off. This is why a kite's axis of symmetry is exactly the diagonal joining the two vertices where equal sides meet.

commonErrors.misconception: Forgetting to state AC = AC (common) — without it there is no third pair and no SSS.

examTip.value: In a congruence proof, always write the two triangles with corresponding vertices in matching order (ABC ↔ ADC) — then every corresponding pair can be read straight off the naming.
